nameStory: The White Synapta gets its name from its pale, translucent white appearance that makes it look almost ghostly in the sand. 'Synapta' comes from Greek meaning 'joined together,' referring to how these sea cucumbers can fragment and regenerate their bodies when threatened.
description: The White Synapta is a slender, worm-like sea cucumber that burrows in sandy and muddy ocean bottoms. Unlike the bumpy sea cucumbers you might find in tide pools, this one looks more like a pale earthworm with a smooth, almost translucent body. It can grow up to 6 inches long but is quite thin, about the width of a pencil. Most people encounter them when they wash up on beaches after storms or when digging for clams.

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Feels smooth and slippery like wet silk, with a translucent white to pale pink color that you can almost see through

idTips.label: Shape and size
idTips.description: Long and thin like a large earthworm, up to 6 inches long but only pencil-thick, tapering at both ends

idTips.label: Fragility
idTips.description: Extremely fragile - will break apart into pieces when handled roughly, unlike tougher marine worms

idTips.label: Surface feel
idTips.description: Completely smooth with no bumps, spines, or ridges - feels almost like handling jelly

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Moves by extending and contracting its body in waves, much slower than most marine worms

habitat: Found in sandy and muddy bottoms of shallow coastal waters from the low tide zone down to about 100 feet deep. They prefer areas with fine sediment where they can easily burrow, often in eelgrass beds and quiet bays along the New England coast. You're most likely to see them washed up on sandy beaches after storms.

seasonality.spring: Begin to become more active as water temperatures rise. Fresh specimens may wash ashore during spring storms.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're feeding and reproducing in the sediment. Best time to find live specimens.
seasonality.fall: Still active but starting to burrow deeper. Storm-driven specimens commonly wash up on beaches.
seasonality.winter: Burrow deep into sediment and become less active. Rarely seen except as beach wrack after major storms.

funFact: When threatened, the White Synapta can literally throw pieces of itself at predators - it breaks off body parts that continue wriggling as decoys while the main body escapes, then regenerates the missing pieces over time!
confusionNotes: Often mistaken for large marine worms or even small snakes when washed up on beaches. Unlike true worms, synaptids feel much more fragile and jelly-like, and will break apart easily when handled. Marine worms are typically tougher and more rubbery.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a sea cucumber, this animal looks nothing like the chunky, warty sea cucumbers most people picture. They're part of the same group (echinoderms) as starfish and sea urchins, but have evolved a completely different body plan for life in soft sediments.
compareHints: The White Synapta is the only common synaptic sea cucumber in New England waters. It differs from other local sea cucumbers by being much more slender and fragile, lacking the tough, warty skin of species like the Orange-footed Sea Cucumber. Unlike those chunky relatives, White Synaptids are specialized burrowers that rarely leave the sediment.
